analysis.one_liner: Ends the Federal Reserve's practice of paying banks interest on their reserve balances.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat untouched in the House Financial Services Committee since its July 2025 introduction, with zero cosponsors and no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-page bill repeals the section of federal law, added in 2008, that authorizes the Federal Reserve to pay interest on the money banks keep on deposit at the Fed — balances that run into the trillions of dollars. Today those interest payments, made under the very paragraph this bill strikes, are the Fed's main tool for steering short-term interest rates. Ending them would stop a risk-free income stream to banks and leave more of the Fed's income to flow to the Treasury, but it would also strip the Fed of the centerpiece of its modern rate-control system.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passes, the U.S. Treasury benefits first: the Fed would stop paying banks for holding reserves and would remit more of its earnings to the federal government, modestly shrinking the deficit. Borrowers could benefit if banks, no longer earning risk-free returns on parked reserves, moved that money into loans. The sponsor frames the payments as a subsidy to banks that ordinary taxpayers effectively underwrite.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The federal Treasury, and possibly borrowers

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes paragraph (12) of section 19(b) of the Federal Reserve Act, the provision that authorizes the Fed to pay interest on reserve balances, effective 180 days after enactment.
Under current law, banks earn interest on the trillions of dollars they hold at the Fed — a risk-free return on money that, its critics argue, could otherwise support lending or federal revenue.

The payments the bill ends are an expense to the Federal Reserve; stopping them would leave more of the Fed's income available to remit to the Treasury, which turns over its excess earnings to the federal budget.

analysis.who_pays: Commercial banks holding large reserve balances lose a risk-free income stream running into the tens of billions of dollars a year. The wider public bears the risk on the other side: interest on reserves is how the Fed currently steers the federal funds rate, so removing it with no replacement could make short-term rates harder to control, with effects that reach every borrower and saver.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks holding reserves; anyone exposed to rate volatility

drawbacks.text: The paragraph the bill strikes is the legal basis for the Fed's primary tool for controlling short-term interest rates under the current 'ample reserves' system; repealing it with no replacement framework could make it harder for the Fed to keep rates where it wants them, affecting mortgages, car loans, and savings rates.

The bill is a one-line repeal that offers no alternative mechanism for monetary control; even observers who agree the payments benefit banks have generally argued for reforming them rather than striking the authority outright.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The fiscal argument is real: banks do collect risk-free interest on reserves, and ending it would redirect money to the Treasury and, in principle, toward lending. But the cost side is serious. The same provision the bill targets is the load-bearing wall of modern Fed rate control, and the bill replaces it with nothing. Repeal could produce rate volatility that hits ordinary borrowers and savers harder than the bank payments ever cost them. On balance, the bill aims at a legitimate grievance with a blunt and risky instrument.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on July 29, 2025 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has received no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Warren Davidson introduced H.R. 4789 in the House on July 29, 2025.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction, and no further action has been taken on it since.
No member of the House from either party has cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, banks that hold reserve balances at the Fed are better off, because the interest payments this bill would have ended continue unchanged. No one else has been affected, since the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Warren Davidson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strike the Federal Reserve's interest-on-reserves authority.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 29, 2025 and has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern has formed.

industries.note: Banks earn risk-free interest on the trillions of dollars they keep on deposit at the Fed, paid under the exact paragraph this bill strikes. Ending it would redirect that money toward the Treasury and, in principle, toward lending, though banks would lose a guaranteed revenue stream.

The Fed would save the expense of reserve interest payments, but it would lose the primary tool it uses to steer short-term rates, leaving it with no stated replacement for the job Congress assigned it.

analysis.trajectory: With one sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no committee action since July 2025, the bill is overwhelmingly likely to die quietly at the end of this Congress without ever receiving a hearing or a vote.
